text: Detection is only half of EDR's name. Once the telemetry, process trees, and LOLBin patterns from this chapter confirm a real compromise, an analyst needs to act on a live machine remotely, without touching it physically. Three actions cover almost every real response: isolating the host, killing the malicious process, and quarantining the file -- and the order and combination matter as much as the actions themselves.

Isolating a host is usually the first move, and it's more precise than shutting anything down: it cuts off nearly all normal network traffic while leaving one secure channel open between the EDR agent and the console. The machine keeps running -- an analyst can still issue commands and watch live telemetry -- but it can't reach a command-and-control server, move laterally, or exfiltrate another byte of data.

The obvious alternative, unplugging or shutting the machine down, is usually the wrong call. Running processes, injected code, active connection state, and encryption keys in use all live only in volatile memory -- RAM -- and none of that survives a power-off. A fileless attack never wrote most of that to disk in the first place, so powering off destroys the only copy of evidence that ever existed, and some malware even erases its own traces the moment it detects a shutdown.

Killing a process remotely stops one confirmed-bad process immediately without taking the whole host offline. Quarantining a file moves or encrypts it so it can no longer run -- the same outcome traditional antivirus always delivered, just issued remotely as one tool in a larger response. Combined with isolation, these three actions let an analyst contain an incident -- stopping the spread -- while keeping the machine live long enough to reconstruct exactly what happened.

That combination -- isolate, kill, quarantine -- is containment in practice, and it closes out this chapter's look at endpoint detection. Next, we move from the endpoint itself to the broader threat intelligence picture: what an indicator of compromise actually is, and the common types a SOC watches for across an entire environment, not just one machine.
